title: A Signal for the Colony
premise: Odile Montrose, a disgraced insurance investigator hiding as the caretaker of an unregistered beacon on the system's edge, is the only witness to a nine-second gravitational flicker that shouldn't be possible. The flicker is the residue of a mass jump: eleven thousand colonists from Meridian Station were erased in transit, and every official record now insists they never existed. When Odile finds a survivor's black box hidden inside his own beacon's foundation, he realizes he was given this post by someone who knew, and that his invisibility was engineered. Racing the closing jump window with a found family of smugglers, a grieving archivist, and the station AI that has begun lying to protect him, Odile must force the truth into the public record before the evidence—and everyone who carries it—is jumped out of existence. He succeeds at terrible cost: the massacre is proven, the beacon burns, and Odile chooses exile over erasure, broadcasting the names of the dead into the dark.
about_author: Quentin Sandoval is the pen name of a former maritime claims adjuster who spent a decade investigating losses at sea before turning to fiction. They write from a coastal town whose location they decline to confirm, citing ongoing litigation.

chapters.title: The Nine Seconds
chapters.summary: POV Odile. During a routine calibration of the forgotten beacon, gravity stutters for exactly nine seconds; every instrument logs it, then every instrument denies it. Odile, who trusts instruments over people, feels the ground of his quiet life shift. Beat: unease disguised as professional curiosity.

chapters.title: Caretaker of Nothing
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Flashback woven through present routine: how a ruined investigator came to maintain a beacon no one claims. We learn he took the job from a faceless contract signed years ago. Beat: loneliness revealed as chosen armor.

chapters.title: The Vessel That Isn't There
chapters.summary: POV Odile. A smuggling ship, the Kestrel's Debt, docks uninvited seeking shelter from a patrol. Its captain, Rhea Okonkwo, recognizes the beacon's signature and goes pale. Beat: first crack in isolation—someone else knows something.

chapters.title: Meridian Station
chapters.summary: POV Rhea. Rhea remembers Meridian Station vividly: she delivered cargo there twice. But charts show empty space, and her own crew doubts her memory. Beat: gaslighting begins; loyalty to her own mind wavers.

chapters.title: The Contract Clause
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Digging into his employment contract, Odile finds a clause paying him double if the beacon 'never requires investigation.' Insurance language as threat. Beat: paranoia sharpened into method—he investigates himself.

chapters.title: Black Box in the Foundation
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Repairing a corroded strut, Odile finds a sealed recorder embedded in the beacon's original foundation, dated the day construction began. It contains a child's voice counting down. Beat: dread—the beacon was built around evidence.

chapters.title: Eleven Thousand Names
chapters.summary: POV Odile. The box holds a partial passenger manifest for Meridian Station: 11,042 souls, none of whom appear in any registry Odile can reach. Among them, a name matching his own mother's maiden name. Beat: personal stakes detonate.

chapters.title: The Archivist Who Grieves
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa Vann. Introduce Ilsa, a records archivist on the hub world Ceres Gate who keeps noticing 'gaps' in her archives—smooth patches where files should be. She files a discrepancy report and is summoned within the hour. Beat: institutional menace.

chapters.title: Questions in a Warm Room
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. Ilsa is interviewed by a courteous man from the Continuity Office who explains that gaps are normal, that her predecessor also worried, and that her predecessor retired. Beat: fear wearing a polite smile.

chapters.title: A Beacon Answers
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Odile broadcasts a query on a dead frequency listed in the black box. Against all odds, something answers: a repeating phrase, 'the window closes in forty days.' Beat: hope arriving like an alarm.

chapters.title: Passage Bought with Lies
chapters.summary: POV Rhea. Odile hires the Kestrel's Debt with money he doesn't have, promising salvage rights to the beacon itself. Rhea agrees against her crew's objections. Beat: found family forming under protest.

chapters.title: The Crew of the Debt
chapters.summary: POV Rhea. Portrait of the crew: engineer Tam, ex-doctor Juno, teenage pilot Wren who was born in transit and has no registered birthplace. Their rootlessness mirrors Odile's. Beat: belonging offered sideways.

chapters.title: Ceres Gate
chapters.summary: POV Odile. The Debt reaches Ceres Gate; Odile sees civilization for the first time in six years and feels its indifference like weather. He seeks the archive where Meridian records should live. Beat: awe curdling to alienation.

chapters.title: Ilsa's Gap
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. Ilsa catches Odile in the restricted stacks; instead of reporting him, she shows him the smooth patch where Meridian Station's entire history used to be. Two investigators recognize each other. Beat: alliance kindled.

chapters.title: What the Smooth Patch Hides
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. Using pre-digital microfilm backups, Ilsa recovers one fragment: a maintenance log mentioning 'transit casualties, containment advised.' Someone chose to erase rather than mourn. Beat: grief as evidence.

chapters.title: The Continuity Office
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Odile tails the courteous man and discovers the Continuity Office's true function: not preserving records but curating reality. His own name appears on a watchlist, flagged 'asset, do not disturb.' Beat: the horror of being managed.

chapters.title: Asset, Do Not Disturb
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Odile realizes his exile was designed: the beacon keeps him alive, isolated, and harmless—a witness in cold storage. Rage replaces fear. Beat: identity crisis—invisible by design or by choice?

chapters.title: Wren's Question
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Wren asks Odile why proving dead people existed matters when the living are barely surviving. Odile has no good answer yet, only that names are the only thing death can't forge. Beat: thematic argument voiced by the youngest.

chapters.title: The Second Flicker
chapters.summary: POV Rhea. Gravity flickers again—four seconds this time—and the Debt's nav systems briefly show a starfield with Meridian Station in it, intact, screaming on open channels. Then gone. Beat: the erased are still dying somewhere.

chapters.title: Transit Purgatory
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Reconstructing the physics, Odile understands: the jump failed mid-transit eleven months ago. The station exists in a folded corridor between points, looping. The nine-second flickers are it knocking. Beat: scale of horror fully grasped.

chapters.title: Containment Advised
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. Ilsa decodes the microfilm further: the Continuity Office didn't cause the accident—it caused the cover-up, sealing the corridor to prevent 'reality drift.' The dead are quarantined. Beat: villainy reframed as bureaucratic mercy.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: POV Odile. The courteous man, Director Hale, meets Odile openly: help us keep the seal stable until the corridor decays naturally, and you'll be rich, restored, remembered. He reveals Odile's mother died at Meridian. Beat: temptation weaponized through grief.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: POV Rhea. Rhea weighs selling Odile out—Hale's offer would buy her crew real lives. Tam votes yes; Wren storms out; Juno abstains. Rhea burns the offer unread. Beat: loyalty chosen over survival, at cost.

chapters.title: Thirty-Six Hours
chapters.summary: POV Odile. The jump window—the natural alignment that could pull the corridor open—closes in thirty-six hours. After that, Meridian loops forever, unreachable, deniable. The plan crystallizes: fly the beacon itself into the fold. Beat: clock starts.

chapters.title: What a Beacon Is For
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Odile confesses to the crew that the beacon was built to amplify exactly the signal needed to anchor the corridor open long enough for rescue. His whole hidden life was a loaded gun. Beat: purpose retroactively revealed.

chapters.title: The Archive Raid
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. Ilsa steals the full Meridian manifest and casualty projections from Ceres Gate, triggering alarms she doesn't evade. She transmits everything to the Debt and lets herself be taken. Beat: sacrifice as testimony.

chapters.title: Interrogation of Ilsa Vann
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. In custody, Ilsa refuses to recant, forcing Hale to either release her (validating the record) or detain her (creating a martyr and a paper trail). She wins by losing. Beat: justice outside the law, fought with procedure.

chapters.title: Hale's Confession
chapters.summary: POV Hale. Interlude: Hale's POV. He was on the review board that sealed the corridor; he tells himself it was triage. He orders the Debt's destruction and hates how much that order costs him. Beat: antagonist humanized, not excused.

chapters.title: Betrayal at the Dock
chapters.summary: POV Tam. Tam, terrified, sells their route to the Continuity Office—not for money but because his sister is on the watchlist too. The ambush at the dock kills Juno. Beat: betrayal born of love; first major loss.

chapters.title: Juno's Empty Chair
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Grief chapter. Wren, who learned medicine watching Juno, takes her kit. The crew nearly fractures; Odile refuses to hate Tam, which is somehow worse. Beat: found family tested by grief.

chapters.title: The Fold Corridor
chapters.summary: POV Rhea. The Debt dives toward the fold point under fire. Physics made visceral: time smears, Wren flies by memory of a place she's never been. Beat: terror and wonder fused.

chapters.title: Meridian Station Found
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Inside the corridor: Meridian Station, frozen in the moment of the accident, eleven thousand people alive in a loop of the same nine seconds. Some have been aware for eleven months. Beat: rescue becomes almost unbearable.

chapters.title: The Loop's Witness
chapters.summary: POV Odile. Odile meets the loop's self-appointed historian, a station teacher named Amara Diallo, who has recorded every iteration. Her archive matches his black box. She asks the question: can you prove we happened? Beat: witness meets witness.

chapters.title: Capacity
chapters.summary: POV Rhea. The brutal math: the corridor can hold open for minutes, not hours. The Debt can carry perhaps three hundred people. Eleven thousand. Rhea must choose who boards. Beat: the moral cliff edge.

chapters.title: Amara's Decision
chapters.summary: POV Amara. Amara organizes the station: the oldest and sickest board first, and volunteers stay to hold the loop stable manually. She stays. 'Prove us,' she says, handing Odile her archive. Beat: dignity in the impossible choice.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: POV Odile. As the evacuation runs, Odile uses the beacon-amplified signal to broadcast the manifest, the microfilm, Ilsa's transmission, and Amara's archive to every receiver in the system. Truth as flood, not argument. Beat: climax ignition.

chapters.title: Nine Seconds, Open
chapters.summary: POV Wren. Hale's ships arrive to reseal the corridor; Wren threads the Debt through them carrying 312 survivors while the broadcast makes killing them politically impossible in real time. The window slams shut behind them. Beat: climax peak—escape through a closing eye.

chapters.title: Aftermath of Light
chapters.summary: POV Ilsa. Released amid public outrage, Ilsa watches the system react: vigils, inquiries, Hale resigning into obscurity, the Continuity Office dissolved. 10,730 names confirmed dead; 312 saved; the arithmetic debated forever. Beat: justice achieved, incomplete.

chapters.title: Tam's Testimony
chapters.summary: POV Tam. Tam testifies publicly about his betrayal, restoring Juno's name to the record alongside the eleven thousand. Rhea doesn't forgive him, but lets him stay aboard. Beat: forgiveness withheld, belonging granted anyway.

chapters.title: A Signal for the Colony
chapters.summary: POV Odile. The beacon burned out anchoring the corridor; Odile rebuilds it voluntarily, no contract, no anonymity. He inscribes Amara's archive into its foundation and leaves the light on—for the next erased station, the next witness. Beat: resolution—visibility chosen, family kept, signal eternal.
